title: Augustine, Boethius, and early Christian thought
note: Early Christian thinkers used Greek philosophy, especially Platonism, to understand their faith. Augustine argued that evil is a privation of good, that God created time with the world, and that grace heals the will. Boethius, writing in prison, argued that true happiness is God and that God's eternal knowledge does not destroy free choice.

read.title: Restless hearts and the wheel of Fortune
text: Augustine of Hippo moved through Manichaeism, which taught that good and evil are rival cosmic powers, before reading the Platonists and then converting to Christianity in 386. The Platonists helped him think of God as immaterial and of evil not as a thing but as a lack. A blind eye is not a new substance; it is an eye missing sight. So the good God created only good things, and evil arises when creatures, especially wills, turn away from the highest good toward lesser ones.
Augustine also asked what God was doing before creation. His answer was that the question assumes time existed before the world, but time is itself a creature. God, eternal, is not in time at all.

A century later Boethius, a Roman statesman unjustly condemned, wrote The Consolation of Philosophy while awaiting execution. Lady Philosophy reminds him that Fortune is a wheel: whoever rides it must expect to fall. Wealth, office, and fame cannot give happiness because they can be lost. Only the highest good, God, can. She also answers a worry about freedom. God's eternity is not a long time but the whole of life possessed at once, so God sees our future acts as we see present ones, without forcing them.
